claims.text: The proposed framework explicitly incorporates oxygen-induced defect scattering and temperature-dependent conductivity descriptors.
The framework will predict thermal and/or electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The physics-informed ML framework will be more accurate than analytical models based on perfect, defect-free crystals.
The 1 wt.% oxygen HfNbTaTiZr specimen contains oxygen interstitials and typical defect structures.
The model will be trained using partial conductivity data, defect-scattering descriptors, and domain-informed regularization.
Oxygen interstitial distributions and resulting short-range defect interactions enhance carrier scattering.
Physics-informed defect-scattering descriptors capture non-ideal conductivity behavior overlooked by conventional models.
The model can learn the effect of oxygen defects on conduction mechanisms across temperature.
The conductivity predictions will fall within approximately 15–20% deviation from measurements.
The accuracy advantage will be greatest in the temperature region where defect scattering dominates.
Existing analytical conductivity models assume defect-free crystals and omit oxygen-induced scattering.
Existing analytical models show significant deviations from experimental HfNbTaTiZr conductivity data in the stated temperature regimes.
The hypothesis is limited to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with 1 wt.% oxygen at 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Applicability outside the stated oxygen content, alloy composition, and temperature intervals is untested.
The magnitude of any improvement may vary with training-dataset quality.
Defect interactions at extremely low temperatures may not be fully captured.
Conductivity will be benchmarked at multiple temperatures from 400 K to 800 K on controlled 1 wt.% oxygen samples.
Deviation exceeding approximately 20% across 400–800 K will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome defines 15–20% as the model's deviation from measurements, whereas the uncertainty field describes 15–20% as the improvement in predictive accuracy. These are different quantities and are treated as though they were interchangeable.

The main hypothesis is comparative—better accuracy than conventional models—but the falsification rule only tests whether the ML error exceeds 20% and never compares its error with a conventional-model control. A model could exceed 20% error yet still outperform the baseline.
